There are no network operations during build or package phases beyond the initial Git clone defined in the source array.

The check() function creates a simple C++ test file, compiles it using the built eccp compiler, and runs it — a reasonable smoke test. All operations are self-contained and use only local resources. The package installs no systemd services, kernel modules, or privileged helpers. The installed eccp script wrapper and configuration files appear to be part of the legitimate toolchain functionality.

This is a standard wrapper script for the EDG C++ front end (edgcpp). It sets up environment variables pointing to the compiler components under `/usr/lib/edgcpp` and then `exec`s the real compiler driver (`$ECCP`, defaulting to `$EDG_BASE/bin/eccp.sh`) with all passed arguments. There is no network activity, no encoded/obfuscated content, no file system manipulation, and no execution of anything other than the package's own declared binaries.

The use of environment-variable overrides (`${ECCP-...}`, `${EDG_BASE-...}`, etc.) is explicitly documented in the script header and is a standard pattern for compiler wrappers — it allows users to redirect to alternate toolchain installations. While an attacker who can set `ECCP` or `EDG_BASE` in the build environment could cause arbitrary code execution, this is a general property of environment-driven build tools and not evidence of a supply-chain attack in the package itself. The `"` sequences are just HTML-escaped quotes from the rendering; the actual file contains ordinary `exec "$ECCP" "$@"`.

No genuinely malicious behavior — no data exfiltration, no downloads, no backdoors, no tampering with system files — was found. The file is consistent with ordinary packaging practice for a compiler front-end wrapper.
</details>
